wording.reason: Minor. Every McKetin element of the statement, magnitude, plain text, population, exposure, comparator, outcome, domain notes and reasoning matches the PDF: 469 people dependent on methamphetamine in Sydney and Brisbane, mostly entering treatment and mostly injecting, past-month reports at entry, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years, 2006–2010 (pp. 2–3); violent crime defined as crime involving violence such as in a robbery or assault (p. 2); 113 of 927 (12%) against 19 of 593 (3%) months; 8.2 (4.2–15.9), 5.3 (2.6–10.7) and 3.4 (1.5–8.0), with the covariates as listed (Table 1 and notes, 2.1.2, p. 3); unadjusted dose percentages only, adjusted dose estimates in an unread supplement (pp. 3–4); same-month self-report, no treatment or imprisonment covariates, an exploratory analysis (p. 3); the authors' statements on wide intervals and on dependent, not recreational, use (p. 5); three authors shared with the birth cohort and four with the review (pp. 1, 6). Odds are correctly called odds. The one sentence that says more than the paper shows is 'which removes the influence of stable personal characteristics': that holds for a fixed-effects estimator, but the abstract says the odds ratios came from a random-intercept model (p. 1) while the methods name the fixed-effects option (p. 3), and a random-intercept model does not by itself remove stable confounding (card reporting issue 0). The review and birth-cohort elements were not re-read in this batch; I relied on their ai-checked anchors.

relation.reason: Rated as an association (METHODS 6.1, 6.3), the relation should follow the adjusted estimates, and every one points the same way: the review's pool 1.4 (0.8–2.4, I² 25%), the birth cohort's perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54) and intimate-partner perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30), and the dependent cohort's within-person violent crime 3.4 (1.5–8.0, p = 0.005; Table 1, p. 3). Two longitudinal studies exclude no association, the second clearly, so 'neither an effect nor its absence can be shown with precision', the protocol's test for insufficient evidence, no longer describes the evidence; the very low rating carries the uncertainty, and the statement already says that causation is not settled. Two cautions belong in the reasoning, as proposed under wording: the review's pool includes the MATES sample, so it adds direction but not independent precision; and the birth cohort's lower limits sit at 1.00–1.04 without adjustment for other illicit drugs, the adjustment that reduced the MATES estimate from 5.3 to 3.4.

status.reason: Fits METHODS 6.4 exactly: two studies in the same direction that share investigators (McKetin, Boden and Foulds are three of the four authors of the birth-cohort paper; McKetin 2020 reference list, p. 6), and the dependent cohort is a sample already inside the review's pool. Mixed no longer fits: it requires inconsistent findings without an adequate explanation, and the adjusted estimates do not conflict (I² 25% in the review's adjusted pool; both cohorts above 1). The remaining inconsistency, violent behaviour 3.7 against violent offending 1.0 in the review's unadjusted post hoc subgroups, concerns unadjusted estimates, and the dependent cohort's association for self-reported crime involving violence, an offending-type outcome, runs against the unadjusted offending null; noting it in the reasoning without labelling the claim by it is right. Replicated (independent) cannot be given, because no independent primary study with an adjusted estimate in the same direction has been read. On the alternative in reader 29's report (keep insufficient evidence, add the McKetin anchors as qualifying): it is defensible only if the birth cohort's marginal, partly adjusted estimates are set aside, leaving MATES as the only clear adjusted association, from a sample already inside a pool whose interval includes 1. Even then, mixed would be the wrong label, because the adjusted findings are not inconsistent; the label would rest only on the unadjusted behaviour–offending split, which the reasoning would have to say. I prefer the main proposal.

justified.reason: A separate claim is justified. McKetin 2020's main results are for crime in general (any crime, dealing, property crime, fraud; abstract and Table 1), which the violence claim does not cover; folding them into it would mix outcomes in a claim that is already long. One within-person cohort read in full, at very low certainty, as a single-study claim, fits the protocol. The two claims should cross-refer, because the any-crime estimate includes the months with violent crime.

wording.proposed: Statement: 'In people dependent on methamphetamine (one Australian cohort of 469 people, most entering treatment in Sydney and Brisbane and most injecting, 2006–2010), months with methamphetamine use, compared with the same people's months without use, are associated with more self-reported crime: any crime in 515 of 927 months with use (56%) against 104 of 593 months without (17.5%). Within-person odds ratios adjusted for age, income, unemployment, unstable housing and other substance use were 4.7 (2.8–8.0) for any crime, 5.9 (3.0–11.9) for drug dealing and 5.5 (2.8–10.8) for property crime; fraud was not clearly associated (1.7, 0.8–3.3); violent crime is in the violence claim (3.4, 1.5–8.0). Adjusting for other substance use reduced the odds ratios by a third to nearly two-thirds; unadjusted percentages rose with days of use, and the adjusted dose estimates are only in a supplement that has not been read. Use and crime were self-reported for the same month in the same interview, so which came first is unknown; treatment and imprisonment during follow-up were not taken into account; the analysis was exploratory, its estimator is described ambiguously and the number of people contributing to each estimate is not reported. The authors limit the findings to people dependent on methamphetamine. Whether use causes crime is not shown.' Magnitude: 'Within-person odds ratios, months with use against the same people's months without (Table 1): any crime 13.2 (8.5–20.6) unadjusted, 10.5 (6.6–16.7) adjusted for age and socio-economic factors, 4.7 (2.8–8.0) also adjusted for other substance use; dealing 18.2 (10.2–32.5), 15.8 (8.6–29.1), 5.9 (3.0–11.9); property crime 10.6 (6.3–18.0), 8.4 (4.8–14.5), 5.5 (2.8–10.8); fraud 3.4 (2.0–5.8), 2.8 (1.6–5.0), 1.7 (0.8–3.3), p = 0.158. Shares of months without against with use: any crime 104 of 593 (17.5%, printed 17%) against 515 of 927 (56%); dealing 6% against 36%; property crime 7% against 30%; fraud 5% against 13%. Unadjusted shares by 0, 1–15 and 16 or more days of use (editors' reading of Fig. 1, no values printed): any crime about 18%, 48% and 71%; dealing 6%, 27% and 53%; property crime 7%, 26% and 39%; fraud 5%, 12% and 16%.'
wording.reason: Every number in reader 29's proposal is right (Table 1, p. 3: 4.7 (2.8–8.0), 5.9 (3.0–11.9), 5.5 (2.8–10.8), 1.7 (0.8–3.3); 515/927 = 55.6%, 104/593 = 17.5%), but the wording is not exact in four places. (1) 'Mostly drug dealing and property crime' reads as the make-up of the crime, which the paper does not report as such (types overlap within a month); what it shows is that dealing and property crime have the largest adjusted odds ratios. (2) Fraud appears in the list of associations without saying that its adjusted interval includes 1 (p = 0.158; the abstract calls it not significant). (3) 17.5% is the editors' figure; Table 1 prints 17%, so the counts should be given. (4) The adjustment is not named, and the main limits are missing from the statement itself, though the violence claim carries them: same-month self-report in one interview, no treatment or imprisonment covariates, an exploratory analysis, an ambiguously described estimator with no count of contributing people, and the authors' restriction to dependent people (pp. 1–5). The fall from Model 1 to Model 2 recomputes to 35% to 63% (10.5 to 4.7, 15.8 to 5.9, 8.4 to 5.5, 2.8 to 1.7). The proposal rightly uses odds ratios rather than the paper's 'times more likely' (pp. 3–4).

relation.reason: An association in one within-person cohort, with adjusted intervals well clear of 1 for any crime, dealing and property crime; causal wording is not supported, because use and crime were reported for the same month (METHODS 6.1).

grade.reason: Starts low. Risk of bias −1: ROBINS-E high on the card (same-interview self-report, unmeasured changes around treatment entry and imprisonment, reverse causation within the month, an exploratory analysis). Imprecision 0: the three associated outcomes have intervals far from 1; the unreported number of contributing people is a reason for caution, not a downgrade. Inconsistency not assessable with one study; indirectness 0 as worded, since the population is restricted to people dependent on methamphetamine. No upgrade for large effect: the adjusted odds ratios are large (4.7–5.9), but the remaining biases can run away from the null (dealing and property crime bring money or drugs, so crime can drive use within the same month, and reports of use and crime in one interview can move together), which METHODS 6.3 excludes. No upgrade for dose-response: the adjusted dose estimates are only in the unread Table S3, unlike the psychosis-dose claim from the same cohort, whose article printed adjusted dose estimates. Low − 1 = very low.

wording.reason: Every number in the statement and magnitude matches the supplement and the report: the enrolment criterion and its contrast with the report's wording (SOM p. 2; p. 602); controls without personal or family history and similar in age and verbal IQ (SOM p. 2, Table S1); 146 and 145 analysed (SOM p. 4); one expected false-positive cluster per map, the overlap of two comparisons with one control group (SOM p. 4); 55% against 12% smokers, 51% and 64% men (Table S1); the grey-matter-only, statistic-free smoking and single-sex re-analyses (SOM pp. 4, 6); the one-tailed, uncorrected familiality tests (SOM p. 5; pp. 602–603); the Table S2 values and the recomputed standardized differences (0.71 to 1.30); F(2,141) = 26.3 and η² 0.27; 94% cocaine and 6% amphetamines, urine positive in all but three, methamphetamine never mentioned (SOM p. 2). The four fixes: (1) 'cannot be traced' overstates; the supplement names none of the non-shared clusters, but Fig. 2A (rendered at 220 dpi) shows decreased-volume clusters in orbital or ventral frontal and insular regions in the dependent siblings only, which is what the review describes; this was the first-pass reading and the card keeps it in key finding 8 and selective_reporting. (2) The permutation test compares the spread of within-pair differences in each measure (SOM p. 5), so it is the measures that are alike within families; whether the abnormality is shared is a further inference (see note). (3) The 51% and 64% are close; the imbalance is the 92% among dependent siblings. (4) The supplement does not say whether age was adjusted for; 'no adjustment described' is what can be checked. In the magnitude, the covariate for FA is not named anywhere (SOM pp. 3–5).

note: Answer to the question set: withdrawing 'fits an additional effect of use' is right. Fig. S2 gives maps only, with no statistics, sample size, threshold, correction or region names (SOM p. 7); years of use rise almost in step with age in this group (onset at 16.5, SD 2.8; age 34.5, SD 7.4), and no adjustment for age or for the 55% with opiate and 26% with alcohol dependence is described; so the maps are as expected under an effect of age or of other dependence as under an effect of stimulant use, and 'fits' adds nothing the data can tell apart. The authors' own reading (p. 602) can be reported as theirs, as proposed. Two further points. (a) The familiality test measures how alike each measure is within sibling pairs; a measure that runs in families in everyone can pass it whether or not the siblings' difference from the controls is real, and the report itself says that brain structure is to a large extent inherited (p. 602), so the test supports family resemblance of the measures, not, by itself, a shared abnormality. (b) With the primary study and its supplement now read, the London et al. (2015) anchor (index 2) adds no independent evidence and differs from the study in places (a hippocampal finding, dependent-only orbitofrontal and anterior insular reductions, no postcentral or superior temporal reduction); its role would be more accurate as qualifies than supports.
